# The Recovering Night

In the early hours of January 17, 1994, a magnitude 6.7 earthquake struck the San Fernando Valley. Freeways collapsed. Power failed across Los Angeles. And in the dark that followed, some residents who stumbled outside reportedly called emergency services to ask about the enormous silvery cloud that had appeared overhead, stretching horizon to horizon.

They were looking at the Milky Way.

This story is told, in various forms, about several blackouts — New York in 1965, the Northeast in 2003 — and it is easy to hear it as a joke about city people, detached from nature. I hear it differently. I hear it as evidence of a severing so complete that the galaxy we live inside has become unrecognizable. Something enormous was restored for a few hours, and people no longer had a name for it.

Daylight is a local broadcast. It shows us our star and almost nothing else — the sun so dominates the sky that every other star, including several hundred shining there invisibly all day, is washed from view. Night is what happens when the local programming goes off the air and the rest of the universe, which was there the whole time, becomes visible. Darkness is not the absence of light. It is the removal of the nearest light, the one that was crowding out everything else.

What fills the gap is staggering, and it used to be ordinary. From a genuinely dark place — a desert, a mountain, the open ocean — the naked eye can pick out about three thousand stars at once, perhaps nine thousand over the whole rotating night. Venus will be unmistakable, often mistaken for a landing aircraft. The band of the Milky Way will arc overhead, brightest toward Sagittarius, where we are looking edge-on into the crowded center of our galaxy, its light riven by the Great Rift, a river of cold dust that is not emptiness but a screen — too much matter, not too little, standing between us and the rest. Off-center in the autumn sky sits a faint smudge you will see better if you don't look at it directly: the Andromeda Galaxy, two and a half million light-years away. The light entering your eye left its source before our species existed. It is the farthest thing you will ever see unaided, and for most of human history people saw it every clear night without knowing what it was — a sister galaxy, adrift, falling toward us at seventy miles a second.

Our ancestors were not casual about any of this. They were professional. The night sky was the first calendar, the first clock, the first map, the first broadcast of origin stories. The Greeks called the planets *planetai* — wanderers — because they refused to hold their places among the fixed stars, and their stubborn motions became the groundwork of astronomy and, eventually, physics. Polynesian wayfinders crossed thousands of miles of open ocean with no instruments, reading star paths and swells memorized as sequences. Aboriginal Australians read constellations in the dark itself: the Emu in the Sky is drawn not in stars but in the shadow of dust lanes, a figure made of darkness unfurling across the Milky Way. Some of the oldest stories on Earth are written in the negative space.

We have been losing this for a long time, but the loss accelerated with the electric light, and it is now nearly total. By the most careful accounting available — a 2016 atlas of artificial sky brightness — more than 80 percent of North Americans and 60 percent of Europeans cannot see the Milky Way from where they live. One-third of humanity cannot see the galaxy it belongs to. From the centers of bright cities the star count drops from thousands to a few dozen. The rest have not gone anywhere. They are behind a veil of our own making: light wasted upward, scattered by the atmosphere into a luminous dome that astronomers call skyglow, a word that sounds like a mild apology.

The cost is not only aesthetic. Hatchling sea turtles emerge from the sand at night and orient toward the brighter horizon, which for millions of years has been the ocean, reflecting sky. Under a beachfront's sodium glow they turn inland and die. Migrating birds, which navigate by stars, are drawn off course into lit buildings. Fireflies, whose entire courtship is a language of darkness, cannot be heard over it. And in humans — who are, whatever we prefer to think, creatures of a formerly dark world — the loss may be subtler and stranger. There is a reason every tradition of awe we have, religious or scientific, reaches for the same vocabulary: vastness, smallness, humility, scale. The night sky is the one experience that reliably produces the feeling psychologists call the sublime, the sensation of meeting something so much larger than yourself that the self temporarily expands to accommodate it. We have been treating that experience as optional. It may be one of the few experiences that tells our nervous systems the truth about where we are.

There is a small movement to take it back. Flagstaff, Arizona, whose dark skies made Lowell Observatory possible, became the world's first officially dark city in 2001, and since then a few hundred places have followed, shielding their lights and reclaiming their stars. The solutions are almost embarrassingly simple — point the light down, use less of it, make it warmer — and they save money. The Milky Way is not a scarce resource in the way oil is scarce. It is an absent one, absent only because we have been careless about where we throw our light.

And it is recoverable in a way few losses are. The stars have not moved. Dim the lights over Los Angeles for a single night — an earthquake will do, or a blackout — and the galaxy reappears over the freeways as if it had been waiting, which it had. Somewhere right now, on a dark stretch of the Pacific, a hatchling turtle is orienting by a sky older than speech. We could stand to join it. The dark is not empty. It is the one place the universe is legible, and it has been there the whole time, patiently, above the noise we made.

**The Recovering Night**

In the early hours of January 17, 1994, a magnitude 6.7 earthquake struck the San Fernando Valley. Freeways collapsed. Power failed across Los Angeles. And in the dark that followed, some residents who stumbled outside reportedly called emergency services to ask about the enormous silvery cloud that had appeared overhead, stretching horizon to horizon.

They were looking at the Milky Way.

This story is told, in various forms, about several blackouts — New York in 1965, the Northeast in 2003 — and it is easy to hear it as a joke about city people, detached from nature. I hear it differently. I hear it as evidence of a severing so complete that the galaxy we live inside has become unrecognizable. Something enormous was restored for a few hours, and people didn't have a name for it.

Daylight is a local broadcast. It shows us our star and almost nothing else — the sun so dominates the sky that every other star, including several hundred that shine there invisibly all day, is washed from view. Night is what happens when the local programming goes off the air and the rest of the universe, which was there the whole time, becomes visible. Darkness is not the absence of light. It is the removal of the nearest light, the one that was crowding out everything else.

What fills the gap is staggering, and it used to be ordinary. From a genuinely dark place — a desert, a mountain, the open ocean — the naked eye can pick out about three thousand stars at once, perhaps nine thousand over the whole rotating night. Venus will be unmistakable, often mistaken for a landing aircraft. The band of the Milky Way will arc overhead, brightest toward Sagittarius, where we are looking edge-on into the crowded center of our galaxy, its light interrupted by the Great Rift, a river of cold dust that is not an absence of stars but too many of them, too close, blocking the view behind. Off-center in the autumn sky sits a faint smudge you will see better if you don't look at it directly: the Andromeda Galaxy, two and a half million light-years away. The light entering your eye left its source before there were humans on Earth. It is the farthest thing you will ever see unaided, and for most of human history, people saw it every clear night without knowing what it was — a sister galaxy, adrift, falling toward us at seventy miles a second. [Check: Andromeda approaching Milky Way at ~110 km/s ≈ 68-70 miles/s. Yes, roughly. Good.]

Our ancestors were not casual about this. They were professional. The night sky was the first calendar, the first clock, the first map, the first broadcast of origin stories. The Greeks called the planets planetai — wanderers — because they refused to hold their places among the fixed stars, and their stubborn motions became the groundwork of astronomy and, eventually, physics. Polynesian wayfinders crossed thousands of miles of open ocean with no instruments, reading star paths, swells, and the rising points of stars memorized as sequences. Aboriginal Australians read constellations in the dark itself: the Emu in the Sky is drawn not in stars but in the shadow of dust lanes, a figure made of darkness that unfurls across the Milky Way. Some of the oldest stories on Earth are written in the negative space.

We have been losing this for a long time, but the loss accelerated with the electric light, and it is now nearly total. By the most careful accounting available — a 2016 atlas of artificial sky brightness — more than 80 percent of North Americans and 60 percent of Europeans cannot see the Milky Way from where they live. One-third of humanity cannot see the galaxy it belongs to. From the centers of bright cities, the star count drops from thousands to a few dozen. The rest have not gone anywhere. They are behind a veil of our own making: light wasted upward, scattered by the atmosphere into a luminous dome that astronomers call skyglow, a word that sounds like a mild apology.

The cost is not only aesthetic. Hatchling sea turtles emerge from the sand at night and orient toward the brighter horizon, which for millions of years has been the ocean, reflecting sky. Under a beachfront's sodium glow, they turn inland and die. Migrating birds, which navigate by stars, are drawn off course into lit buildings. Fireflies, whose entire courtship is a language of darkness, cannot be heard over it. And in humans — who are, whatever we prefer to think, creatures of a formerly dark world — the loss may be subtler and stranger. There is a reason that every tradition of awe we have, religious or scientific, reaches for the same vocabulary: vastness, smallness, humility, scale. The night sky is the one experience that reliably produces the feeling psychologists call the sublime, the sensation of encountering something so much larger than yourself that the self temporarily expands to meet it. We have been treating that experience as optional. It may be one of the few experiences that tells our nervous systems the truth about where we are.

There is a small movement to take it back. Flagstaff, Arizona, whose dark skies made Lowell Observatory possible, became the world's first officially dark city in 2001, and since then a few hundred places have followed, shielding their lights and reclaiming their stars. The solutions are almost embarrassingly simple — point the light down, use less of it, make it warmer — and they save money. The Milky Way is not a scarce resource in the way oil is scarce. It is an absent one, absent only because we have been careless about where we throw our light.

And it is recoverable in a way few losses are. The stars have not moved. Turn off the lights over Los Angeles for a single night — an earthquake will do, or a blackout — and the galaxy reappears over the freeways as if it had been waiting, which it had. Somewhere right now, on a dark stretch of the Pacific, a hatchling turtle is orienting by a sky older than speech. We could stand to join it. The dark is not empty. It is the one place the universe is legible, and it has been there the whole time, patiently, above the noise we made.
